newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia land row seen sparking right-wing revolt.
newsitem.headline: Australia land row seen sparking right-wing revolt.

text.p: A leading Australian conservative warned on Wednesday of an unprecedented right-wing revolt unless the government abolished indigenous land rights to end a dispute between farmers and Aborigines.

Queensland state premier Rob Borbidge said growing opinion poll support for race row politician Pauline Hanson would turn against Prime Minister John Howard's Liberal-National government at the next election.

"Unless we get a satisfactory outcome to the (land rights issue), the very thing that we are now seeing in the polls will be repeated in ballot boxes around Australia and we will see a revolt from the right that this country has never witnessed before," Borbidge said in a radio interview.
Borbidge, whose state is the most affected by Aboriginal land claims, has been leading a campaign for the government to abolish "native title" on traditional farm land.
But Aborigines are also pressuring Howard, with one negotiator on Tuesday repeating long-running threats to lobby black nations to boycott the 2000 Sydney Olympics.
Howard scolded the negotiator on Wednesday, saying such threats damaged the Aboriginal cause.
"I say to the Aboriginal people, with the best will in the world, stop talking like that," Howard said.
"Every time they open their mouths and they talk like that, they lose further support within mainstream Australia."
The boycott call was also rejected on Wednesday by a senior Aboriginal leader who said it was not being considered by the main Aboriginal group negotiating land rights.
"Our...working party is not talking about those things at the present time," said land negotiator Charles Perkins.

The native title legislation was introduced by the former Labor government three years ago but became an urgent political issue when the High Court decided last December that land leased to farmers for generations could also be liable to claims.
Howard pledged on Monday to impose a compromise deal against opposition from farmers, Aborigines and his own political allies, including Borbidge.
Borbidge said polls showing increasing support for Hanson's One Nation Party had hardened his opposition to Howard's plan.

A newspaper poll on Wednesday said 28 percent of voters would consider supporting Hanson's party in parliament's upper house, the Senate, where minor parties and independents traditionally hold the balance of power.
Such support could make One Nation the third political force after the Liberal-National coalition and Labor.

Hanson, an independent federal parliamentarian from Borbidge's conservative state, sparked a divisive race debate last year when she said Australia was in danger of being over-run by Asians and Aborigines were receiving favoured treatment at the expense of whites.

Key elements of Howard's blueprint include confirming farmers' rights to land they have leased since European settlement began more than 200 years ago, but guaranteeing Aborigines limited access for traditional purposes.
It also reduces Aboriginal rights to negotiate over development and other uses of land and exempts cities, towns and water catchments from Aboriginal claims.
